title: Hand-Rolled Hash Table
statement:
Build a map from integer keys to integer values without using any built-in hash map or hash set (no Map, Set, plain-object lookup tables, dict or set). Arrays and lists are allowed.

  • IntMap() creates an empty map.
  • put(key, value) stores value under key, replacing any value already there.
  • get(key) returns the value stored under key, or -1 if the key is absent.
  • remove(key) deletes key and its value if present; otherwise it does nothing.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the map. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: 3 and 1003 may land in the same bucket, but each keeps its own value. A second put on key 3 overwrites instead of adding a copy.
Removing an absent key is harmless, and a removed key can be stored again. A value of 0 is a real value, not "missing".

constraints: At most 100 000 calls in total to put, get and remove
hints: Keys are bounded. What is the simplest structure that maps a small integer to a slot?
If you cannot afford one slot per possible key, use a fixed number of buckets and send each key to bucket key % B. Two keys can share a bucket.
Each bucket is a short list of [key, value] pairs. put updates the pair if the key is there or appends it; remove deletes the pair.

explain.intuition:
A hash map is an array of buckets plus a rule that turns a key into a bucket index. Here the rule can be as simple as key % B for a fixed prime B such as 2 069. Different keys can land in the same bucket (a collision), so each bucket holds a small list of [key, value] pairs and you scan that list for the exact key.

With 100 000 keys spread over about 2 000 buckets, each list stays around 50 entries, which is fast enough. A real implementation grows the bucket array when the lists get long (the load factor), which keeps every operation O(1) on average. Because the keys here are bounded by 10⁶, a plain array with one slot per key also works; it trades memory for zero collisions.
steps: Pick a bucket count B (a prime spreads keys more evenly) and create B empty lists.
put(key, value): find bucket key % B. If a pair with this key is in it, overwrite the value; otherwise append [key, value].
get(key): scan the bucket for the key and return its value, or -1.
remove(key): scan the bucket; if the key is there, delete that pair (swap it with the last pair and pop for O(1) removal).
pitfalls: Appending a second pair on put for a key that already exists, so a later remove leaves the old value visible.
Using 0 or a falsy check to mean "absent", which breaks for a stored value of 0.
Picking a bucket count that shares factors with common key patterns (like 1 000 for keys that are multiples of 1 000), which piles everything into a few buckets.

complexity.time: O(n / B) per operation, O(1) on average with resizing

solutions.title: Direct-address array
solutions.idea: Keys are at most 10⁶, so give every possible key its own slot and use -1 for empty.

solutions.title: Buckets with separate chaining
solutions.idea: key % B picks a bucket; each bucket is a small list of [key, value] pairs that is scanned for the exact key.

followups: Keys can now be any 64-bit integer or a string. What hash function would you use, and when would you resize?
Replace chaining with open addressing (linear probing). How does remove work without breaking later lookups?
